mainTopic: Proving ownership of land: admissions, מיגו against witnesses, an incomplete חזקה, claims about produce, and a חזקה with only one witness
overview: This עמוד opens with the last words of an earlier story: once a relative admitted he was not the closer heir, he is bound by that admission and must pay. Then two people each claim a field came from their ancestors. One brings witnesses about his ancestors, and the other brings witnesses that he used the field for the years of חזקה. רב חסדא backs the one using the field with a 'why would he lie' (מיגו) argument, but אביי ורבא hold that a מיגו does not work against witnesses. Next, a man claims he bought a field but can prove only two years of use. רב נחמן rules that the land and the produce he ate both go back to the owner. רב זביד adds that if he had claimed he only bought the produce, he would be believed, because people are not brazen enough to openly eat what isn't theirs. The גמרא explains that land needs a document of sale, but produce sales usually don't. Finally, a man brings only one witness to his three years of use. The students before אביי compare this to רבי אבא's case of snatched metal, and that story begins, with רבי אמי's ruling continuing on the next עמוד.

steps.title: An admission settles the earlier case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the reasoning of the earlier story. Once the relative admitted he was not the closer heir, that admission counts against him.
steps.whatsHappening: These three words close the previous story on the earlier דף. The relative admitted he was not the closer heir, so the admission obligates him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By admitting someone else was the closer relative, he also admitted that he never had a right to the fruit. So by his own words he has to pay. Nobody needs to prove anything more against him.

keyTerms.meaning: An admission, which binds the person who makes it

steps.whatToRemember: A person's own admission works against him. Once he admitted he was not the closer heir, he also admitted he had no right to the fruit.

phrases.english: Since he admitted, he admitted.
phrases.notes: The 'he' is the relative from the earlier story, who admitted someone else was closer to the one who died.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the reasoning of the story that began before this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Once he admitted he was not the closer heir, he is bound by that admission and has to pay.

steps.title: Two people each claim the land came from their ancestors
steps.stepSummary: A new case: each person says the land is an inheritance. One brings witnesses about his ancestors. The other brings witnesses that he used the land for the years of חזקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one says: it belonged to my ancestors. That one says: it belonged to my ancestors. This one brought witnesses that it was his ancestors' land. That one brought witnesses that he used it for the years of חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new case so it can ask who wins. The ruling comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side has witnesses, but they prove different things. The first side's witnesses prove where the land came from. The second side's witnesses prove that he held and used it for three years, which is normally enough for a חזקה.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'ate': used the land and enjoyed its produce
The years (three) needed to set up a presumption of ownership

phrases.english: This one says: 'It belonged to my ancestors,'
and that one says: 'It belonged to my ancestors';
this one brought witnesses that it was his ancestors',

phrases.aramaic: וְהַאי אַיְיתִי סָהֲדִי דַּאֲכַל שְׁנֵי חֲזָקָה –
phrases.english: and that one brought witnesses that he used it for the years of presumption –

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה אוֹמֵר: ״שֶׁל אֲבוֹתַי״, וְזֶה אוֹמֵר: ״שֶׁל אֲבוֹתַי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case, separate from the admission story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the case is set up here. The ruling follows in the next step.

steps.title: רב חסדא: the one using the land wins, because why would he lie
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules for the one who used the land. He could have made a stronger claim ('I bought it from you'), so we believe the claim he actually made.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: Why would he lie? If he wanted to lie, he could have said: I bought it from you and used it for the years of חזקה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא answers the case and backs the person who used the land. His tool is 'why would he lie' (a מיגו).
steps.deeperAnalysis: With three years of use, the man could have said 'I bought it from you,' and that claim would have won. Since he could have won with that easy claim, we believe him when he says 'it was my ancestors'.

keyTerms.meaning: Why would he lie? He could have won with a different claim
The general name for this 'he could have claimed something better' argument

phrases.english: Rav Ḥisda said:
Why would he lie?
If he wanted, he could have said to him:
'I bought it from you'
'and I used it for the years of presumption.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא: מָה לוֹ לְשַׁקֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the case set up in step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The one with witnesses to three years of use wins, through a מיגו: he could have claimed he bought the land.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מיגו makes the possessor believable here.

steps.title: אביי and רבא: no 'why would he lie' against witnesses
steps.stepSummary: אביי ורבא disagree with רב חסדא. A מיגו cannot help a claim that witnesses contradict.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי ורבא do not agree with רב חסדא. We do not say 'why would I lie' where there are witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי ורבא reject רב חסדא's reasoning. A מיגו does not work when witnesses contradict the claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here witnesses said the land belonged to the other man's ancestors. That directly contradicts the claim 'it was my ancestors.' A מיגו can make an unproven claim believable, but it cannot beat a claim that witnesses have already shown to be false.

keyTerms.meaning: Where there are witnesses (against the claim)
We do not say (this rule does not apply)

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי ורבא, a מיגו (מה לי לשקר) does not work against witnesses.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a basic limit on מיגו that shows up in many places: a 'he could have said better' argument cannot win against witnesses.

phrases.english: Abaye and Rava do not hold
this view of Rav Ḥisda –
'Why would I lie'
where there are witnesses, we do not say.
phrases.notes: The witnesses here are the ones who said the land belonged to the other man's ancestors.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּיֵי וְרָבָא לָא סְבִירָא לְהוּ הָא דְּרַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב חסדא's ruling in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using a מיגו in this case at all.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Witnesses contradict the possessor's claim, and a מיגו cannot override witnesses.

steps.title: A man claims he bought the land but proves only two years
steps.stepSummary: A story: a man claims he bought the land and used it for the years of חזקה. He can only bring witnesses for two years.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: What are you doing with this land? He answered: I bought it from you and used it for the years of חזקה. He went and brought witnesses that he used it for two years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story to set up רב נחמן's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חזקה needs three years of use. By saying 'I bought it from you,' the man agrees the land used to belong to the other person. Now he must prove the purchase through a full חזקה, but his witnesses cover only two years.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his fellow:
What do you want with this land?
He said to him: I bought it from you,
and I used it for the years of presumption.
He went and brought witnesses
that he used it for two years.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ לְחַבְרֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בְּהַאי אַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about a חזקה that falls short.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the case is set up here. רב נחמן rules in the next step.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the land and the produce go back
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that the land goes back to the original owner. The man must also pay back the produce he ate during the two years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The land goes back, and the produce goes back.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן decides the story: the man with only two years loses the land. He also has to repay what he took from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He admitted the land used to belong to the other person, and he could not prove the purchase with three years. So the land is treated as the original owner's all along. That means the produce he ate was not his, and he must pay for it.

keyTerms.meaning: It goes back (returns to the owner)

steps.whatToRemember: An incomplete חזקה proves nothing. The land returns, and so does the value of the produce eaten.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think two years earns 'partial credit,' letting him keep the produce he already ate. Without a full חזקה he has no proof at all, so even the produce must be paid back.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
The land goes back, and the produce goes back.
phrases.notes: 'The produce goes back' means he pays the owner for what he ate during those two years.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הָדְרָא אַרְעָא, וְהָדְרִי פֵּירֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the story in step 5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: With only two years proven, the man has no חזקה. The land and the value of its produce go back to the original owner.

steps.title: A claim of only eating the produce is believed
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד rules that if the man claimed he only came onto the land to eat its produce, he is believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: If he claimed, 'I went onto the land to eat the produce,' he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד adds a limit to רב נחמן's ruling about paying back the produce. If the man had claimed he only bought the right to eat the produce, he is believed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן made the man return the land and pay back the produce he ate. רב זביד says the payment depends on the claim. If he said from the start that he only bought the produce, we believe him, and he doesn't pay for what he ate.

keyTerms.meaning: He claimed (made a claim in court)
I went onto the land for the produce (I only bought the right to eat the fruit)

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said:
If he claimed and said
phrases.notes: This is the man from the story just before, who could only show two years of using the land.

phrases.english: "I went down onto the land for the produce" – he is believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב נחמן's ruling that the produce must be paid back
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who claims he only bought the right to eat the produce is believed, so he doesn't pay for the produce he ate.

steps.title: Proof from the man with the sickle
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד's ruling is supported by רב יהודה's rule that a man who says he bought someone's dates and goes to cut them is believed, because people are not that brazen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Didn't רב יהודה say: Someone holding a sickle and a rope who says, 'I'm going to cut the dates of so-and-so's tree, because he sold them to me,' is believed? So a person is not brazen enough to cut down dates that aren't his. Here too, a person is not brazen enough to eat produce that isn't his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up רב זביד with a ruling of רב יהודה about a man who openly goes to cut someone's dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה's rule rests on one idea: people don't openly take fruit that isn't theirs. The same idea applies to someone who openly ate the produce of a field. So when he says he bought the produce, we believe him.

keyTerms.meaning: A rope used for climbing a date tree
A person is not so brazen

phrases.english: Didn't Rav Yehuda say:
This one who is holding a sickle and a rope,
and says: I will go cut the dates
of the date tree of so-and-so,
who sold it to me – he is believed?
phrases.notes: He means the dates were sold to him, not the tree itself.

phrases.english: Apparently, a person is not so brazen
that he would cut a date tree that is not his;
here too, a person is not so brazen
as to eat produce that is not his.

steps.raayaObject: רב זביד's ruling that a claim of buying only the produce is believed
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יהודה's ruling about a man who goes to cut someone's dates and says they were sold to him

steps.title: Then believe him about the land too
steps.stepSummary: If people aren't brazen enough to take what isn't theirs, why not believe him that he bought the land itself?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, believe him about the land too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reasoning it just used. If people don't openly take what isn't theirs, the same should be true for the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea that 'people aren't that brazen' seems to prove too much. It would mean anyone working a field is believed when he says he bought it, even without a full חזקה. That goes against רב נחמן's ruling that the land goes back to the owner.

phrases.english: If so, the land as well!
phrases.notes: He means: let him also be believed that he bought the land itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning of the proof
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning that 'a person is not so brazen'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If this reasoning works, it should also make him believed about owning the land, which contradicts רב נחמן.

steps.title: For land we ask to see a document
steps.stepSummary: For land, we tell him to show his document of sale.
steps.simpleTranslation: For the land, we say to him: Show us your document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that land is different. Someone who buys land gets a document, so we ask to see it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With land, the normal proof is a document of sale. If he doesn't have one, his claim is weak, and 'people aren't brazen' is not enough to save it.

phrases.english: Regarding the land, we say to him:
Show your document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about the land
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'not brazen' reasoning should also make him believed about the land.
steps.terutzMaskana: For land, people expect a document of sale, so without one he is not believed.

steps.title: Then ask for a document for the produce too
steps.stepSummary: If we ask for a document for land, we should ask for one for produce as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, ask for a document for the produce too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. Why not demand a document for the produce as well?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If missing paperwork makes a claim weak, he should need a document to prove he bought the produce too. Then רב זביד's ruling would fall apart.

phrases.english: If so, the produce as well!
phrases.notes: He means: let us also say to him, 'Show your document for the produce.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer about the document
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that we ask to see a document
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If we ask for a document for land, the same demand should apply to produce.

steps.title: People don't write documents for produce
steps.stepSummary: People don't usually write documents when they buy only produce, so a spoken claim is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: People don't usually write a document just for produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a produce sale is normally done without any paper. So we don't expect him to have a document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule follows what people normally do. Land sales come with a document, so having none weakens the claim. Produce sales don't come with one, so having none means nothing, and the 'not brazen' reasoning stands.
steps.whatToRemember: A claim of buying only the produce is believed, because people aren't brazen enough to openly eat what isn't theirs, and no one writes documents for produce. For land, we expect a document.

phrases.english: A document for produce
people do not make.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge and closes the discussion of רב זביד
steps.terutzResolutionType: Based on what people normally do
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A document should be needed for produce too.
steps.terutzMaskana: People don't write documents for produce, so lacking one doesn't weaken the claim.

steps.title: A land claim with only one witness
steps.stepSummary: A man says he bought a field and used it for the years of חזקה, but he brings only one witness to the three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man said to another: What are you doing on this land? He answered: I bought it from you, and I used it for the years of חזקה. He brought one witness that he used it for three years.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. The man on the land has his full three years, but only one witness to prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the problem was that his proof covered too few years. Here the years are complete, but the proof is weak: one witness instead of the usual two. The question will be how the court rules.

keyTerms.meaning: The years needed to show ownership (three years)

steps.confusionAlert: One witness is not a full proof in court. That is why this case is unclear, even though the three years are complete.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to another:
What do you want with this land?
He said to him: I bought it from you,
and I used it for the years of presumption.
He brought one witness
that he used it for three years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case after the discussion of רב זביד
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the case: a full three years of use, but only one witness.

steps.title: The students compare it to רבי אבא's metal case
steps.stepSummary: The students before אביי think this case is just like רבי אבא's case of the snatched metal.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן sitting before אביי wanted to say: This is the same as רבי אבא's case of the piece of metal.
steps.whatsHappening: The students suggest an earlier case that should decide this one. This line sets up the next step, where that case is told.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases have one witness on one side. The students think the ruling from רבי אבא's case should carry over to the land case. Whether the comparison really works will be checked later.

phrases.english: The Rabbis before Abaye thought to say:
This is the case of the cast metal of Rabbi Abba –

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Suggests an earlier case that should decide the land case
steps.raayaObject: The ruling in the one-witness land case
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אבא's case of the snatched metal

steps.title: The story of the snatched metal
steps.stepSummary: A man snatched metal from another. One witness saw it. The snatcher admits it but says the metal was his own. רבי אמי begins to rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man snatched a piece of metal from another. The case came before רבי אמי, and רבי אבא was sitting with him. The victim brought one witness that it was snatched from him. The snatcher said: Yes, I snatched it, but what I snatched was mine. רבי אמי said:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells רבי אבא's case so we can compare it to the land case. It stops just as רבי אמי is about to rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here, too, there is only one witness. The snatcher doesn't deny grabbing it. He only says it belonged to him. רבי אמי's ruling comes next, and it will decide whether the comparison helps the land case.

phrases.english: For there was a certain man
who snatched a piece of cast metal from another.
He came before Rabbi Ami,
phrases.notes: The one who came to court is the man whose metal was taken.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Abba was sitting before him.
He brought one witness
that it was indeed snatched from him.
The other said to him: Yes, I snatched it –
but what I snatched was mine.
Rabbi Ami said:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells the earlier case that was just mentioned
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sets up the metal case: one witness to the snatching, and the snatcher admits grabbing it but says it was his. רבי אמי's ruling follows.
